query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In pre-exposed Q235 steel, the stability of its native iron oxide layer determines whether corrosion-related degradation is initiated or suppressed. At room temperature, the naturally formed, relatively coherent passive oxide layer serves as an effective barrier against chloride ion attack, whereas at elevated temperatures, thermal expansion and stress induce microcracking or delamination of this oxide, exposing fresh metal and thereby accelerating localized corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 carbon steel in its as-received (pre-exposure) state with its native/mill-scale iron oxide present from standard processing.
generation.intervention: Expose identical Q235 steel samples to a harsh, chloride-rich aqueous environment (e.g., 0.5 M NaCl solution) at two different temperature regimes—room temperature (~25°C) and an elevated temperature (e.g., ~70–90°C).
generation.conditions: Testing in a controlled laboratory setup under identical chloride concentration, pH, and oxygenation conditions; one set maintained at room temperature and the other at a defined elevated temperature representative of potential service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The continuity and adhesion of the native iron oxide passive layer on the steel surface.
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, the passive iron oxide layer remains intact and limits ingress of aggressive chloride ions. When exposed to elevated temperatures, thermal stress leads to microstructural disruption (e.g., microcracking, spallation) of the oxide film, facilitating chloride penetration and rapid localized corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples maintained at room temperature will exhibit minimal corrosion (low mass loss, low pitting density), while those at elevated temperatures will show significant disruptions in the oxide layer (observable via microscopy), increased corrosion current densities, and higher mass loss and pitting intensity compared to the untreated reference.
generation.baseline: Q235 steel kept under ambient storage conditions with an intact native oxide layer typically shows very low corrosion rates in benign environments.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate in environments where the temperature is elevated enough to induce thermal stresses (e.g., 70–90°C) without causing complete breakdown of the oxide, and in chloride-rich, oxygenated aqueous solutions. Extreme conditions (very high temperatures or aggressive acids) may introduce additional corrosion pathways beyond oxide breakdown.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature threshold at which the native oxide becomes unstable and the quantitative change in corrosion rate remain to be determined. Other factors such as mechanical stress, humidity, or minor compositional variations in the native oxide may also influence the corrosion behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of Q235 steel specimens in their pre-exposed state and subject them to immersion in a 0.5 M NaCl solution while maintaining two controlled temperature conditions (room temperature ~25°C versus elevated temperature ~70–90°C). Use identical solution chemistry and exposure periods. Monitor the surface oxide integrity through surface microscopy and spectroscopic analysis both before and after exposure, while quantifying corrosion rates via weight loss measurements and electrochemical techniques (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization, EIS).
measurements: Surface oxide layer continuity and integrity (using SEM/optical microscopy)
Corrosion current density and polarization behavior (via electrochemical measurements)
Mass loss after a fixed immersion period
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Q235 samples exposed at elevated temperatures do not exhibit statistically significant (e.g., >20% increase) deterioration in oxide integrity and accelerated corrosion rates compared to the room temperature samples, then the hypothesis that thermal disruption of the native oxide drives enhanced corrosion would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Effects of Cold Rolling or Precipitation Hardening Treatment on the Microstructure, Mechanical Properties, and Corrosion Resistance of Ti-Rich Metastable Medium-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractTitanium-rich metastable medium-entropy alloys, designed for low elastic moduli, sacrifice strength. However, enhancing their mechanical strength is crucial for bio-implant applications. This study aims to enhance the mechanical properties and corrosion resistance of a metastable Ti80–Nb10–Mo5–Sn5 medium-entropy alloy using various treatments, including cold rolling (at 50% and 75% reduction) and precipitation hardening (at room temperature, 150 °C, 350 °C, 550 °C, and 750 °C). The results showed that the alloy underwent a stress-induced martensitic transformation during the rolling process. Notably, the α phase was precipitated in the β grain boundaries after 30 days of precipitation hardening at room temperature. The yield strengths of the alloy increased by 51% and 281.9% after room-temperature precipitation and 75% cold rolling, respectively.
